Proposition 40
Imposes One-Time Tax on Certain Taxpayers. Initiative Constitutional Amendment and Statute.
Analysis of Measure
Background
California Is Home to Many Billionaires. Several of the wealthiest people in the world live in California. Wealth is the value of all the things a person owns. Wealth is different from income, which is how much a person earns in a set period of time, like one year. A person's wealth typically is measured by their net worth. A person's net worth is the value of all the things they own, like stocks, businesses, or other investments, minus their debts. California is home to a few hundred people with net worth over $1 billion, often called billionaires. Many of these billionaires gained their wealth as executives or investors in California technology companies.
Health Care Is a Major Category of State Spending. The state and federal government spend over $200 billion per year on state health care programs. Most state health care spending is for Medi-Cal, the state's health insurance program for low-income people. State spending also supports public health programs, mental health care, and drug and alcohol treatment.
Proposal
Establishes One-Time Wealth Tax on Billionaires. Under Proposition 40, billionaires who were residents of California on January 1, 2026 would have to pay a one-time state tax equal to 5 percent of their net worth. The tax would be due in 2027. Taxpayers would have the option to spread the payments over five years but would have to pay more to do so. Real estate, pensions, and retirement accounts generally would be excluded from the tax.
Most of the Money Must Be Spent on Health Care. The state would decide how and when to spend the money from the wealth tax, but it would have to be spent on certain types of services. Ninety percent of the money would have to be spent on health care services for the public. The rest would have to be spent on education, food assistance, and administration of the wealth tax. Existing rules in the State Constitution that limit spending and require the state to spend a certain amount on schools and community colleges would not apply to this money.
Potential Interactions With Other Propositions
If Proposition 41 or 42 on this same ballot receive more "yes" votes than Proposition 40, then Proposition 40 could be stopped from becoming law even if it gets yes votes from a majority of voters. This is because the courts could find that Proposition 41 or 42 conflict with Proposition 40.
Fiscal Effects
Temporary State Revenue Increase From Wealth Tax. The state probably would collect tens of billions of dollars from the wealth tax. This temporary increase in state tax collections would be spread across several years. Exactly when and how much the state would collect is very hard to predict for many reasons. For example, it is hard to know what actions billionaires would take to reduce the amount of tax they pay. Also, much of the wealth is based on stock prices, which are always changing.
Possible Ongoing Decrease in State Income Tax Revenues. California billionaires, like all those earning money in the state, currently pay state taxes on their annual income. Billionaires may respond to a new wealth tax in ways that reduce their income tax payments. For example, some billionaires may decide to leave California. The income taxes they currently pay to the state also would go away. These responses probably would reduce state revenues by less than $1 billion per year. This could mean less money for the state's General Fund, which is the account that pays for most public services, including education, health care, and prisons.
State Costs to Administer the Wealth Tax. The state would have costs to determine how much wealth tax is owed and to collect tax payments. These costs could be tens of millions of dollars per year for several years. These costs would be paid from the new wealth tax revenues.
Yes/No Statement
A YES vote on this measure means: The state would collect a one-time tax from billionaires equal to 5 percent of their wealth.
A NO vote on this measure means: The state would not collect a one-time tax from billionaires equal to 5 percent of their wealth.
Summary of Legislative Analyst's Estimate of Net State and Local Government Fiscal Impact
Temporary state revenue increase from a new wealth tax on billionaires. These wealth tax revenues probably would add up to tens of billions of dollars spread over several years.
Possible ongoing decrease of less than $1 billion per year in state income tax revenue collected from billionaires.
Ballot Label

WEALTH, TAXES, AND WEALTH TAX REVENUE ESTIMATES

California Billionaires: Wealth, Taxes, and Wealth Tax Revenue Estimates
Jasper Boll, Emmanuel Saez, and Gabriel Zucman
NBER Working Paper No. 35218
May 2026, Revised July 2026
JEL No. H20
ABSTRACT
This paper documents the wealth of California’s billionaires and the taxes they pay. California
billionaires’ wealth exceeds $2 trillion today, the equivalent of 50% of California’s GDP. It has grown
144% from 2023 to 2025, fueled by the AI boom. Over the longer run, the real wealth of California’s
billionaire class—the 0.0002% richest households—has been multiplied by 38 from 1982 to 2026,
while average real family income in California has about doubled. California billionaires pay about
0.2% of their wealth in California income tax ($3.2 billion/year), representing 2.4% of total California
income tax revenue on average over 2023-2025. Using Securities and Exchange Commission data from
Alphabet, Meta, Oracle, and Nvidia since 2004, we estimate the trajectory of wealth, income, and
taxes paid by the top 4 California billionaires—Page, Brin, Zuckerberg, Ellison (through 2020), and
Huang (since 2021)—focusing on their business wealth. This group alone holds nearly $1 trillion in
business wealth, about 40% of total California billionaire wealth. For this group, wealth growth
(+322% over 2023-2025) and low taxation (0.04% of wealth in annual California income tax) are more
pronounced. The proposed one-off California billionaire tax of 5%, payable over 5 years, is both small
relative to California billionaires’ wealth gains and large relative to the taxes they currently pay. We
estimate that it could raise about $100 billion, with comparatively minor impacts on income tax
revenue. Using empirical estimates of mobility responses to wealth taxation, we find that an annual
wealth tax on California billionaires could raise substantial additional revenue even after accounting
for income tax losses due to mobility.
Jasper Boll
Paris School of Economics
jasper.boll@psemail.eu
Emmanuel Saez
University of California, Berkeley
Department of Economics
and NBER
saez@econ.berkeley.edu
Gabriel Zucman
Paris School of Economics
and University of California, Berkeley
and also NBER
zucman@berkeley.edu
All the results and computations in excel format is available at
https://eml.berkeley.edu/~saez/BSZ_MainTablesFigures.xlsx
A California Billionaire Wealth Tracker is available at https://cabillionairetracker.org/
1
The 2026 Billionaire Tax Act initiative will be put on the ballot as Proposition 40 for the November
2026 elections in California. The primary goal of the initiative is to raise revenue by imposing a
one-time 5% wealth tax on California billionaires to offset the large federal cuts to Medicaid
(government funded health insurance for low-income families) and other programs enacted by
the Trump administration and Congress in July 2025 (the act is called HR1 or OBBBA).
In principle, the state could undo the federal spending cuts with additional California tax
revenue, but it is challenging for the California government to raise taxes as it requires 2/3
supermajorities in the legislature (since Proposition 13 was adopted in 1978). Hence, in recent
decades, tax and spending increases in California have been driven primarily by ballot initiatives.
The California billionaire tax initiative fits this pattern.
This ballot initiative has generated intense interest in the public debate. The reason for
targeting specifically California billionaires for new revenue invoked by proponents is simple: their
wealth has grown fast in recent years and decades and they currently pay low taxes relative to
their large wealth gains. As a result, taxing billionaires can both raise substantial revenue and
restore tax progressivity at the very top. At the same time, opponents worry that California
billionaires may leave the state, expecting such wealth taxes to be renewed, possibly reducing
future income tax revenue to the state, and its economic dynamism as the engine of tech
innovation.
This paper presents a number of statistics to help illuminate this debate. Using Forbes
billionaire data, we obtain seven main findings.
First, California billionaires’ wealth has grown 144% in the last 3 years (2023-5). The total wealth
of the 250 California billionaires listed by Forbes now stands at $2.3 trillion (as of July 1st 2026),
about half of California annual GDP.
Second, since 1982 and controlling for price inflation, the wealth of California’s billionaire class
(top .0002% richest families) has grown at 8.5% per year on average while average family income
in California has grown at 1.4% per year. Hence, while Californians income has doubled on
average since 1982, billionaire class wealth has been multiplied by 36.
Third, in recent years 2023-2025, we estimate that California billionaires pay about 0.2% of their
wealth in California individual income tax or about $3.2 billion total per year which is 2.4% of all
California income tax revenue or 1% of total local and state California taxes.
Fourth, using Securities and Exchange Commission data, we estimate that the top 4 richest
(Page, Brin, Zuckerberg, Huang) pay .07% of their wealth or $0.27 billion total each year in
2
California individual income tax (average over 2019-2025) on their company wealth (Alphabet,
Meta, Nvidia). In 2019, 2020 and 2023, Page and Brin did not pay California individual income
tax on their Alphabet wealth as they did not sell stock, received no dividends, and received no
compensation, while their share of Alphabet profits was about $10 billion each over these 3 years.
Fifth, including all taxes at all levels of government, we estimate that California billionaires pay
about 1.1% of wealth in total taxes each year (2023-2025) which is modest relative to their
average annual wealth gains of about 30% in each of those years.
Sixth, we estimate that a 5% one-time wealth tax on California billionaires can raise about $100
billion which is large relative to taxes billionaires pay yet small relative to their wealth gains, with
comparatively modest income tax losses due to potential mobility.
Seventh, we estimate that a permanent wealth tax on California billionaires can raise substantial
revenue even taking into account mobility responses estimated from economic studies of regional
wealth taxes.
The paper is organized as follows. In Section 1, we document California billionaire wealth growth
in both the short-term and long-term. In Section 2, we estimate the taxes paid by California
billionaires. In particular, we show that Securities and Exchange Commission data can provide a
very granular and accurate picture of the wealth, income, and taxes paid by the top 4 centi-
billionaires (Larry Page, Sergei Brin, Mark Zuckerberg, and Jensen Huang) whose wealth is
almost entirely derived from publicly traded stock from the companies they founded or run
(Alphabet/Google for Page and Brin, Meta/Facebook for Zuckerberg, and Nvidia for Huang).
Section 3 draws from the empirical literature on wealth taxation to analyze the prospects of taxing
billionaires wealth as a one-time tax (in Section 3.1) or as a permanent annual tax (in Section
3.2).
1 California Billionaires Wealth Growth
In this section, we document the growth of California billionaires’ wealth, first in the short-run since
2019 and second in the longer-run since 1982 using Forbes billionaires’ data. Forbes has
developed a sophisticated methodology to find and track billionaires’ wealth. Forbes
systematically uses Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) data to track down ownership
of publicly traded stock as large shareholders (owning 5% or more of a company) and company
insiders (board of director members or executive officers) are required to report their ownership
3
and stock transactions to the SEC. This form of wealth is 2/3 of total billionaires’ wealth in
California today and is extremely well measured.
Short-run billionaire wealth growth
The Forbes real-time billionaire list provides daily data on the wealth of all California billionaires
identified by Forbes since 2019. We include both US and non-US citizens California residents
(according to Forbes) in our estimates. There are 250 CA billionaires with total wealth of $2,300
billion by July 1st, 2026.2
Table 1 Panel A provides basic statistics on California billionaires in recent years.
Appendix Table A1 provides the same statistics at the US level (instead of California). Figure 1
plots the trajectory of California’s billionaires’ total wealth (in nominal current dollars) at the end
of years 2019 to 2025 and for July 1st, 2026. This is the longest time series we have for all
California billionaires. It also plots the wealth trajectory of the top 4 (Larry Page, Sergei Brin, Mark
Zuckerberg, and Jensen Huang) who are centi-billionaires (wealth above $100 billion). Larry
Ellison is excluded from these series throughout the 2019 to 2026 period for consistency.3 The
reason for considering this top 4 group specifically is because they account for 40% of the total
CA billionaire wealth (as of July 1st, 2026). This shows that wealth is also very concentrated within
the billionaire class itself. Furthermore, because the wealth of the top 4 is overwhelmingly (97%
at the end of 2025 to be precise) from the publicly traded corporations they founded and/or still
run (Alphabet for Page and Brin, Meta for Zuckerberg, and Nvidia for Huang), the Securities and
Exchange Commission (SEC) public disclosures allow us to estimate precisely their wealth, their
income, and the taxes they pay on their company wealth. Their example illustrates very well the
steep upward wealth trajectory and the comparably low taxes they pay. The top 4 are also taking
part in the public debate on the California billionaire tax. Larry Page and Sergei Brin are
considering leaving California because of the tax and Sergei Brin has contributed to the campaign
against the tax. Mark Zuckerberg has also bought real estate in Florida which may signal a future
move as well.
2 This is a revised estimate relative to the one provided in Galle et al. (2026a) as it excludes Larry Ellison whom Forbes
lists as California resident until mid-January 2026. Forbes magazine reported on February 27, 2026, that Ellison made
a public declaration of domicile in Florida already in May 2023 (Liu 2026). Hence, we perform an ex-post correction
to the Forbes list by discarding Larry Ellison as California resident following his change of domicile. Appendix section
A provides detailed information on the estimation of California billionaire wealth.
3 According to Forbes, he left for Hawaii in late 2020 and then moved to Florida in 2023 (see above). He was almost
surely a California resident for tax purposes in 2019 (and before).
4
Panel A in Figure 1 shows that California billionaire wealth risen sharply over the last 3
years 2023-2025 growing from $843 billion at the end of 2022 to $2,055 billion at the end of 2025.
This is a growth of 144% in just three years. Annual growth was 31% in 2025, 36% in 2024 and
37% in 2023 (Table 1, Panel A). It has grown a further 12% in the first half to 2026. By July 1st,
2026, California billionaire wealth is 52% of the projected California GDP for 2026, up from 23%
in 2022. This means that the 250 California billionaires could buy about half of what California’s
economy has produced during year 2026. It is a useful measure of the weight of billionaires
relative to the size of the entire economy. We keep track of California billionaires’ wealth on a
daily basis here.
Table 1 shows that wealth in the form of large holdings of publicly traded stock reported
through SEC forms is 65% in 2025 up from 47% in 2022. From now on, we call such SEC reported
publicly traded stock as public stock wealth. We call the remaining wealth “private wealth”
because it is comprised primarily of large stakes in private businesses (although it also includes
all other forms of wealth including financial wealth in the form diversified stock holding, bonds,
etc.). This distinction is important because wealth from large publicly traded stock holdings is both
easy to spot (as it is reported to the SEC) and easy to value (as the stocks trade publicly). The
large fraction of such public stock wealth in California is in large part driven by the top 4 who
account for 43% of total CA billionaire wealth (as of the end of 2025) and whose wealth is almost
entirely comprised of publicly traded stock. Panel B in Figure 1 depicts the industry composition
of California billionaires’ wealth with a breakdown between SEC reported publicly traded stock vs.
other for each industry (as of the end of 2025). In California, the tech sector accounts for 73% of
total California billionaires wealth, of which 80% reflects wealth in the form of publicly traded stock.
The next largest industry is finance (which includes venture capital, private equity, and crypto
currency in addition to traditional finance) which is 14% of the total (and divided half and half
between SEC reported publicly traded stock wealth vs. other). The remaining industries comprise
only 13% of the total and are mostly from private businesses rather than publicly traded
businesses.
Panel A in Figure 1 shows that this upward wealth trajectory is even more extreme for the
top 4 whose wealth grows from $209 billion (end of 2019) to $882 billion (end of 2025), a 322%
increase, over the same three years (Table 1, Panel A). Top 4 wealth is $948 billion as of July 1st
2026, 41% of total CA billionaire wealth. The large growth in recent years is tied to the boom in
Artificial Intelligence that drove up the stock prices of the large tech companies owned by the top
4 all of which are heavily involved in the AI boom: Alphabet (gemini AI), Nvidia (chips
manufacturing), and Meta (Meta AI and infrastructure).
5
Longer-run surge in billionaire wealth
This short-run wealth increase is the extension of a much deeper and longer phenomenon of
billionaires’ wealth growth. We use the Forbes 400 richest Americans list compiled annually by
Forbes magazine since 1982 to document the long-run surge of the wealth of the “billionaire class”
US wide and in California in particular. For 2026, we use the Forbes real-time list as of July 1st.
Over such a long-run period from 1982 to 2026, it is important to control for population growth,
roughly doubling over this period, and for price inflation, roughly tripling over this period, and
economic growth (real incomes per family roughly doubling). To control for population growth, the
simplest is to define the “billionaire class” as a fixed fraction of all US or California families, namely
the top .0002% richest families.4 This is about the richest 400 families today US wide and the
richest 45 richest families in California. This is the largest group we can capture with the Forbes
400 data that goes back to 1982.
To control for both price inflation and real economic growth, we compare the “billionaire
class” wealth to the size of the economy, US annual GDP or the California annual GDP, i.e. the
full value of everything produced in the US or California in a year. While wealth is a stock while
GDP is a flow, this is the simplest way to measure the weight of the “billionaire class” relative to
the size of the economy. Table 1, Panel B reports basic statistics on long-run growth of the
California billionaire class wealth and compares it with the growth of California GDP per family
(appendix Table A1 reports the same numbers US wide).
Figure 2 depicts the full time series. Panel A depicts the trajectory of top .0002% wealth
(top 45 families in California today) in 2026 $ billions vs. the trajectory of California GDP per family
(the average economic product of families in California) in 2026 $100,000s. Both series therefore
control for price inflation. California GDP per family has doubled (in real terms controlling for price
inflation) from about $100,000 in 1982 to about $200,000 in 2026. Top .0002% wealth has grown
by a factor 36 from slightly less than $1 billion in 1982 to $36 billion in 2026 (see Table 1, Panel
B for exact values). As a result, California GDP per family looks almost like a flat line relative to
the extraordinary growth of the billionaire class.

the US and in California relative to the size of the economy (US annual GDP and California annual

its dependent children if any and also counting families who do not file income tax returns. In 2025, there are 193
million families US wide and 22.3 million families in California.
6
GDP) from 1982 to 2026. It shows an extraordinary and long-run rise of the weight of the top
.0002% billionaire class in the economy. The top .0002% wealth was about 2% of GDP (both in
the US and in California) in the early 1980s. By 2026, it is 23.5% in the US, a ten-fold increase
and 36% in the California, a 18-fold increase. While there are peaks due to the stock-market cycle,
notably the dot-com bubble in 2000 (particularly in California), the 2007 peak just before the Great
Recession, the post-COVID rally in 2021, and the AI boom in recent years (particularly strong in
California), the underlying trend is strongly upward and hence not tied to the boom and bust of
the stock-market or the tech sector.
Another way to read this evidence is to compute the long-run annual growth rates of
billionaire class wealth vs. average incomes economy wide as done in Table 1, Panel B. From
1982 to 2026 and controlling for price inflation, the average real wealth of families in the top
.0002% increased each year on average by 8.5% in California (6.9% US wide). In contrast,
average real income per family increased only by 1.4% in California (1.3% US wide). Therefore,
California billionaire class wealth has grown 7.1 percentage points faster per year than average
family incomes in California (5.6 percentage points US wide). Such large annual differential

Blue Sky Consulting Group Economic and Fiscal Impacts of the Billionaire Tax Act
James Paci (https://www.blueskyconsultinggroup.com/team-member/james-paci) · Shawn Blosser (https://www.blueskyconsultinggroup.com/team-member/shawn-blosser) · Matthew Newman (https://www.blueskyconsultinggroup.com/team-member/matthew-newman)
September 14, 2026
Prepared by the Blue Sky Consulting Group
This report was prepared by James Paci, Shawn Blosser, and Matthew Newman for the Service Employees International Union – United Healthcare Workers West. The analysis presented and the conclusions of this report are those of the authors.
Read the full report ↓
Contents

Acknowledgements
This report was prepared by James Paci, Shawn Blosser, and Matthew Newman for the Service Employees International Union – United Healthcare Workers West. The analysis presented and the conclusions of this report are those of the authors.
Executive Summary
The Billionaire Tax Act (“BTA”) would assess a one-time 5% wealth tax on California billionaires, generating an estimated $116 billion in revenue for the State of California, or $23.2 billion annually for five years. 1 Over this period, the expenditure of wealth tax revenues is estimated to support over 216,000 wage and salary jobs in California annually—including nearly 150,000 direct jobs in the health care, food assistance, and education sectors—and $45.7 billion in annual economic output. This activity would in turn generate, in addition to the direct wealth tax revenue, an estimated $1.4 billion annually in personal income, corporation and sales tax revenue for the state and local governments.
Available data suggest that the measure's filing has not affected California’s business climate (contrary to claims made by the BTA’s opponents): across measures of early-stage investment, total venture capital funding, and business formation, the state’s share of national activity has held steady or increased since the measure’s introduction in October 2025. Moreover, even under aggressive assumptions regarding the responsiveness of California’s billionaires to the BTA’s one-time wealth tax, revenue losses attributable to the potential departures of some of the state’s billionaires are modest relative to the revenues raised by the measure.
Estimation of Wealth Tax Revenue Generated by the BTA
The BTA would assess a one-time 5% tax on the total net worth, excluding directly held real estate, of billionaires who were residents of California as of January 1, 2026 (i.e., the “tax obligation date”). For purposes of calculating tax liability, the measure specifies that each billionaire’s taxable net worth will be valued on December 31, 2026 (i.e., the “valuation date”).
The BTA is Expected to Generate $116.2 Billion of Wealth Tax Revenue
According to the Forbes Real-Time Billionaires List (the “Forbes List”), as of August 15, 2026, California was home to 261 billionaires who together held a collective net worth of approximately $2.34 trillion. 2 As a result, after excluding the share of this wealth comprised of directly held real estate (an estimated 0.6% of total net worth), 3 the BTA’s one-time 5% wealth tax would generate an estimated $116.2 billion to fund BTA initiatives. Because the BTA allows billionaire taxpayers to spread their tax liability over five equal annual installments, it is expected that expenditures of wealth tax revenue will also be distributed over a five-year period. Therefore, this report’s estimates of the BTA’s annual economic and fiscal impacts reflect an estimated $23.2 billion of BTA expenditures annually (i.e., $116.2 billion divided by five years).
Sensitivity of Revenue Estimate to Billionaire Undercounting and Tax Avoidance
Due to uncertainty regarding the potential underestimation of billionaire net worth, the undercounting of billionaire residents of California, and billionaires’ avoidance of the tax through changes in residency, the baseline estimate of the total billionaire net worth subject to the wealth tax (i.e., $2.34 trillion as of August 15, 2026) may understate or overstate the actual tax base.
Underestimates of net worth and undercounting of billionaires – The estimated number and wealth of California’s billionaires used in this report are based on the Forbes List. While Forbes provides the only publicly available data source identifying all taxpayers potentially subject to the BTA, a recent comparison of Forbes’ and Bloomberg’s ranking of the 500 richest people notes that, due to differing methodologies for estimating net worth, Bloomberg’s net worth estimates for California’s billionaires are, on average, 7.5% higher than Forbes’ estimates. 4
Separately, statistical analysis of the distribution of Forbes List billionaires by Boll et al. (2026) suggests that the list excludes many billionaires with net worths of less than $5 billion. If the estimated combined net worth of these “missing” billionaires is included in the BTA’s estimated tax base, wealth tax revenue would increase by $24.6 billion (or 21.2% of the baseline). 5
Together, these two adjustments to Forbes’ net worth estimates would combine to generate a 30.2% increase in the wealth tax base above the baseline estimate. 6
Wealth tax avoidance – Because the wealth tax is imposed only on individuals who were California residents as of the measure’s January 1, 2026, tax obligation date, the BTA could raise less than $116 billion if some of the state’s billionaires established nonresidency, for state tax law purposes, prior to this date. Since the measure’s filing in October 2025, news reports have identified five California billionaires who took steps to relocate to other states prior to January 1, 2026; these individuals account for roughly $588 billion of the $2.34 trillion of total California billionaire net worth, or approximately $29.2 billion of future wealth tax revenue. 7 Additionally, some observers have noted that the wealth tax could be deemed a “retroactive” tax prohibited by the United States Constitution. If such a challenge were successful, a court could effectively shift the tax obligation date to Election Day, resulting in a further reduction of wealth tax revenue. 8 News reports have identified four billionaires with a combined net worth of $218 billion— equivalent to $10.8 billion of wealth tax revenue—who announced California departures after January 1, 2026. 9
However, given the difficulty of establishing non-residency under California tax law, the impact of these reported departures on wealth tax revenue is highly uncertain. A taxpayer’s California residency depends on a wide-ranging assessment of the taxpayer’s connection to the state during the relevant tax period, and taxpayers bear the burden of establishing that they have “substantially severed” their connections to California. In making this determination, the Franchise Tax Board (FTB) considers the totality of a taxpayer’s connections to the state, evaluating factors such as physical presence, the location of family members, professional and business relationships, and property holdings, among other factors. 10
Based on reports published since the BTA’s filing, three of the five billionaires who announced departures before January 1, 2026 (Larry Page, Sergey Brin, and Peter Thiel), as well as one of the four reported post-January 1 departers (Mark Zuckerberg), have retained relevant connections to California. 11 This group collectively accounts for 95% of the $807 billion of total net worth held by all nine individuals who have left the state.
Figure 1 shows wealth tax revenue estimates under various assumptions as to the total California billionaire tax base and billionaire tax avoidance. If none of the state’s billionaires avoid the tax by establishing non-residency, the BTA would generate $116.2 billion of revenue based only on the Forbes-estimated net worth of billionaires identified by Forbes as of August 15, 2026 (i.e., the baseline revenue estimate). If the total estimated net worth of missing billionaires is added to the Forbes-estimated tax base, wealth tax revenue increases to an estimated $140.8 billion (i.e., $116.2 billion plus $24.6 billion from the missing billionaires). Finally, if the wealth tax base is further adjusted to reflect Bloomberg’s higher average net worth estimates, the state would collect $151.4 billion (i.e., a 7.5% increase on $140.8 billion).
The state would collect less wealth tax revenue to the extent some billionaires are able to avoid the wealth tax. The low-end revenue estimates in the final row of Figure 1 reflect the assumption that a court will move the tax obligation date to Election Day and that, as a result, all nine identified departures are able to establish non-residency. In this scenario, estimated wealth tax revenue decreases to $76.2 billion if only Forbes-identified billionaires are included (i.e., $116.2 billion less the $40 billion generated by these nine departures). 12 However, if missing billionaires are included and Bloomberg’s wealth adjustment is adopted, estimated revenue increases to $108.3 billion.
Figure 1 – Sensitivity of Wealth Tax Revenue (bil 2026 $) to Tax Base and Wealth Tax Avoidance Estimated Wealth Tax Revenue (Aug 15, 2026 Valuation)
Wealth Tax Avoidance Scenario Forbes-Identified Billionaires (Forbes Tax Basis) Including Missing Billionaires (Forbes Tax Basis) Including Missing Billionaires (Bloomberg Tax Basis)
No Billionaires Establish Nonresidency $116.2 $140.8 $151.4
Pre-January 1 Departures Avoid Wealth Tax Entirely $87.0 $111.6 $120.0
Election Day Obligation Date; All Identified Departures Avoid Tax $76.2 $100.8 $108.3
Economic and Fiscal Impacts of BTA Expenditures
The state’s expenditures of wealth tax revenue on health care, food assistance, and education programs would generate a net increase in economic activity and employment statewide.
BTA Economic Impact Estimates
Because billionaire wealth is predominantly held in appreciating assets rather than converted into annual consumption, the wealth tax would draw almost entirely on funds that would not otherwise have entered the California economy. As a result, the net increase in spending on goods and services under the BTA is approximately equal to the amount of wealth tax revenue raised each year. 13
Of the estimated $23.2 billion generated by the BTA annually over five years under baseline assumptions, an estimated 0.7% share, or $170 million, would cover BTA administrative costs such as tax enforcement. 14 The BTA directs 90% of the remaining revenue, or $20.77 billion annually, to support health care services and 10%, or $2.31 billion, to food assistance and education programs. 15 These expenditures comprise the “direct” economic effects of the measure. The recipients of direct spending (e.g., hospitals, schools) support new direct jobs in the health care, food assistance, and education sectors. As shown in Figure 2, the BTA is expected to support nearly 150,000 direct jobs across the health care, food assistance, education, and program administration spending categories. 16
Figure 2 – Annual Direct Spending and Direct Jobs Supported by BTA Policy Category BTA Policy Category Direct Spending (2026 $bil) Direct Jobs
Health Care $20.77 133,199
Food Assistance & Education $2.31 15,848
BTA Program Administration $0.17 509
All Categories $23.25 149,556
As the direct recipients of BTA funding pay their employees and purchase goods and services from suppliers (e.g., medical equipment, school supplies), additional “multiplier” output and employment will be generated across the state’s economy. First, the suppliers of direct BTA recipients pay their workers and purchase their own inputs from other suppliers. Second, the employees and proprietors of these direct and supplier firms support additional employment in other sectors by spending their income at local businesses (e.g., at restaurants or retail establishments). 17 The BTA’s net economic impact includes both direct and multiplier effects.
As shown in Figure 3, over the five-year period, BTA-funded services are estimated to support over 216,000 wage and salary jobs, including the nearly 150,000 direct jobs summarized in Figure 2 (above) and 67,000 additional multiplier jobs throughout the state. 18 Across all jobs supported, the estimated average annual compensation is roughly $85,700. The total annual economic output from this activity is an estimated $45.7 billion (i.e., $23.2 billion of direct BTA expenditures annually plus $22.4 billion of multiplier output at supplier firms and establishments serving these firms and their workers).

Figure 4 shows estimates of the total jobs (direct and multiplier) supported across three industry sector categories. BTA funding is estimated to support a total of nearly 145,000 health care sector jobs and over 16,000 food assistance or education sector jobs over the five-year period. Across all other sectors, the BTA is estimated to support over 55,000 jobs annually.

Fiscal Impact of BTA Expenditures
In addition to the BTA’s economic impacts, the direct services and multiplier activity supported by the BTA would generate tax revenue for state and local governments. First, the wages and income earned by employees, proprietors, and corporations would generate personal income tax (PIT) and corporation tax revenue for the state. Second, the portion of business and labor income that is spent on taxable goods would generate sales tax revenue for both the state and local governments.
As shown in Figure 5, direct and multiplier economic activity supported by BTA expenditures is estimated to generate $1.04 billion annually in PIT, corporation tax, and sales tax revenue for the state General Fund, and $385 million of sales tax revenue annually for California’s local governments. In total, across both state and local governments, the measure would generate $1.42 billion annually. 19

Total Tax Revenue $1,040 $385 $1,425
Potential Economic and Fiscal Impacts of Billionaire Departures
The wealth tax revenue generated by the BTA could be partially offset by the loss of tax revenue associated with billionaires who depart the state because of the BTA’s approval (“mobility losses”). Previous mobility loss estimates put forward by BTA critics have included tax revenues generated by billionaires who have reportedly already left California. However, while the measure’s filing may have caused some billionaires to leave the state, changes in the state’s tax base prior to Election Day are not properly attributable to the BTA’s approval. Instead, for California voters concerned about the BTA’s economic and fiscal impacts, what matters is the extent to which enacting the measure would either result in these individuals not returning to California or cause additional billionaires to leave the state.
Because the BTA imposes a one-time rather than permanent wealth tax—and because an individual’s exposure to this one-time tax is determined based on residency status prior to Election Day—BTA approval would not create a financial incentive to leave the state. Nevertheless, this report estimates the maximum total mobility loss that would result from enacting the measure under an upper-bound assumption as to billionaires’ responsiveness to the Election Day outcome.
The BTA’s opponents have raised two potential sources of mobility loss:
• Business investment losses: Some BTA commentary has suggested that if billionaires leave California,
the state’s start-ups will receive less angel and venture capital investment, resulting in a loss of the economic activity and tax revenues generated by these businesses. Based on available start-up investment and business formation data, however, there is no evidence that the measure’s filing or the billionaire departures to date have influenced capital investment or business location decisions. • Personal income and consumption losses: To the extent that the BTA results in fewer billionaires
residing in California, the measure’s approval would deprive the state General Fund and local governments of the income and sales tax revenue associated with these individuals and their consumption of taxable goods and services in California. Even under upper-bound assumptions as to billionaires’ responsiveness to the BTA’s approval, however, these income and consumption losses are modest relative to the fiscal benefits generated by the BTA.
Billionaires Are Unlikely to Leave (or Return to) California Due to the BTA’s Approval (or Rejection)
Previous estimates of tax revenue losses under the BTA have included revenues generated by billionaires who have already announced departures from California. 20 To the extent that billionaires may have responded to the BTA’s filing by leaving the state, however, these losses have only reduced the state’s pre-Election Day (or status quo) tax base; the fiscal impacts of pre-Election Day departures are not, by definition, a result of voters’ approval of the measure. Instead, the magnitude of the mobility loss under the BTA depends on the post- Election Day behavioral responses of two California billionaire cohorts:
• Pre-Election Departers : To the extent that some of the billionaires who have already left California will
choose to return to California only if the BTA is rejected, approval of the BTA would effectively deprive California’s state and local governments of the tax revenues generated by these individuals’ California residency. • Pre-Election Remainers : Conversely, most of the California billionaires identified by Forbes have
remained California residents. To the extent that some of these billionaires will leave the state if the measure passes, the loss of state and local tax revenues associated with these individuals would constitute a mobility loss attributable to the BTA.
Because the BTA’s wealth tax is imposed on a one-time basis—and because an individual’s tax exposure depends on their residency status prior to Election Day—the measure’s approval is unlikely to provoke a significant migration response from either cohort. Should the measure be enacted, billionaires who have already departed from California will not incur any tax loss if they choose to return to the state after Election
Day. 21 Moreover, none of the billionaires identified in news reports as having left California have suggested that they would return to the state if the measure fails.

Should California tax billionaires? How McClatchy Editorial Board sees Props. 40, 41 & 42
By McClatchy Media’s California editorial boards
October 27, 2026 11:24 AM
A float balloon featuring Mr. Monopoly was featured by San Diego demonstrators in 2021, an example of mounting frustration aimed at the wealthy. On the November election ballot in California, Proposition 40 seeks to impose a one-time tax on billionaires to fund healthcare in the state.
Rob Nikolewski
TNS
Opinion journalists for McClatchy Media conducted interviews with supporters and opponents of all 14 statewide propositions on your November ballot. The journalists then deliberated and decided how they would vote on each one, just as voters do. Proposition 40, the so-called billionaire tax, is the most controversial proposition on the ballot. Prop. 41 and Prop. 42 seek to nullify Prop. 40. In the articles linked below, the journalists explain their positions.
Proposition 40: A one-time wealth tax tied to federal cuts
Prop. 40 would impose a one-time, 5% tax on the wealth of Californians worth more than $1 billion. Ninety percent of the proceeds would be reserved for healthcare; the remaining 10% would go to education, food assistance and tax administration.
The Bee’s endorsement (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/election-endorsements/article317269166.html) is anchored to a specific fiscal threat. According to the California Budget & Policy Center, President Donald Trump’s federal budget bill — known as H.R. 1 — contains the largest cuts to healthcare and food assistance in U.S. history. The center estimates Medi-Cal cuts alone could cost California tens of billions of dollars and cause about 1.3 million Californians to lose healthcare access by 2030. KFF and the Commonwealth Fund have warned the federal cuts could force rural hospitals, community health centers and safety-net medical centers to shed workers and eliminate services, with those institutions standing to lose billions in revenue.
The revenue projections for Prop. 40 vary dramatically depending on who is modeling. Proponents predict about $100 billion. The nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office projects California would probably collect only tens of billions. Stanford economist Joshua Rauh and other Hoover Institution researchers estimate the tax would collect roughly $40 billion — but claim it would ultimately cost California $25 billion, because they believe billionaires will leave the state, taking future income and capital gains tax payments with them.
The LAO, by contrast, projects behavioral changes — including the possibility of billionaires leaving California to avoid the tax — would probably reduce future state revenues by less than $1 billion annually.
The editorial board acknowledges California’s dangerous reliance on volatile revenues from its wealthiest residents, and the endorsement was not unanimous. But a majority concluded that waiting for a perfect federal fix is untenable while coverage disappears. “Billionaires have every right to fight a tax that could cost them billions,” the board wrote. “But voters should recognize the enormous political power that such wealth can buy and ask why so much of that power has been exercised through campaign committees rather than direct public engagement.”
Prop. 40 will almost certainly face litigation, particularly over its provision applying the tax to billionaires who were California residents on Jan. 1, 2026 — months before voters decide the measure. Courts have upheld many tax laws with retroactive provisions, but survival is not guaranteed. Proponents told the editorial board they anticipated litigation and built an accelerated judicial review process into the initiative itself.
The board’s conditional support comes with a demand: every Prop. 40 dollar should be publicly traceable through an online dashboard showing collection, allocation, which providers and programs received funds, and whether the spending actually preserved coverage, access and health outcomes. Lawmakers, the board argues, should use the breathing room to devise the permanent solution Prop. 40 cannot deliver.
Prop. 41: Transparency framing, nullification mechanics
Prop. 41 (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/election-endorsements/article317122476.html) is marketed as a constitutional amendment adding transparency and accountability to ballot measures for special taxes — mandating audits for voter-approved special taxes and ongoing reviews every four years.
The editorial board calls this framing insidious. Prop. 41 is supported by Building a Better California, funded by Google co-founder Sergey Brin and other CEOs and entrepreneurs. One of its most important provisions would ban taxes on or after Jan. 1, 2026, that are exempt from state spending limits — and Prop. 40, as written, is exempt from state spending limits.
That is the mechanism. If Prop. 41 collects more “yes” votes than Prop. 40, its provisions prevail under the California Constitution, and Prop. 40 is effectively voided.
“What’s insidious Prop. 41 is that it is presented as a good governance measure when it’s really about defeating Prop. 40,” the collective editorial boards wrote. The concern is asymmetric visibility: Prop. 40 has drawn significant attention, while Prop. 41 has not — exactly the dynamic a sophisticated nullification campaign would want.
The endorsement (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/election-endorsements/article317122476.html) urges a no vote.
Prop. 42: The 401(k) decoy
Prop. 42 (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/election-endorsements/article317166989.html) is pitched as a safeguard for personal property and 401(k) accounts, barring new state taxes on those assets and restricting certain retroactive taxes. The editorial board describes it bluntly as a poison pill.
The suggestion that any governor would raid middle-class retirement accounts, the board writes, is implausible — any governor who tried “would soon be unemployed.” Even the Legislature, which the board characterizes as inclined to spend more than it should, “knows not to mess with your 401(k).” Opponents also note it appears to be an unsettled legal question whether retirement accounts can be taxed at all, because no government has tried.
Prop. 42 would embed its restrictions in the California Constitution, leaving voters as the only route to change them. The board argues it would create “the illusion of permanently settling California tax policy on financial assets and other personal property” while in fact restricting the state’s future tax options — until the next constitutional amendment or competing voter-approved measure altered that policy.
The real function is familiar: if Prop. 42 collects more “yes” votes than Prop. 40, the wealth tax does not take effect.
“Prop. 42 is a poison pill designed to derail the real debate over a one-time wealth tax on billionaires,” the editorial board wrote. “Voters should reject the decoy and vote no.”
The summary points above were compiled with the help of AI tools and edited by journalists. The source reporting referenced above was written and edited entirely by journalists.

(d) At the time a return is filed pursuant to Section
18501, relating to the filing of an income tax return, for
the 2026 tax year, every California resident individual
required to file shall do either of the following:
(1) Declare that the individual’s net assets were worth
less than or equal to one billion dollars
($1,000,000,000) as of the valuation date.
(2) Submit a declaration of the amount of any
additional tax that is owed under this part, together with
any forms created by the board for calculating any
additional tax owed under this part, along with any
required appraisals or other evidence of fair market
value. In the case of an applicable individual who is not
required to make a return under Section 18501, that
individual shall submit, at the time and in the manner
for filing otherwise required for the making of an income
tax return, the declaration, forms, appraisals, or
evidence described in this paragraph.
(e) Board audit responsibility.
(1) The board shall examine all returns submitted in
accordance with this part and shall determine the
correct amount of the tax under this part. The board
shall also examine all certifications or returns of
taxpayers when the board reasonably believes the
taxpayers should have paid the tax imposed by this part.
Without limiting any other powers of the board, in
examining the returns made by taxpayers and
examining whether returns should have been made by
taxpayers but were not, the board has all powers
provided in Section 19504.
(2) Notwithstanding the previous paragraph, the board
retains the authority to use its sound discretion as to
the length and nature of the examination that is
appropriate under the circumstances.
CHAPTER 2. COMPUTATION OF NET WORTH
50302. Genuine debts and other liabilities owed by
the taxpayer shall be taken into account for purposes of
determining the taxpayer’s net worth. In addition, debts
and liabilities shall be taken into account subject to the
following limitations:
(a) Recourse debts for which the taxpayer is fully
personally liable, without any limitations other than
those arising from bankruptcy law, shall be fully taken
into account.
(b) In the case of debts other than recourse debts
described in subdivision (a), for each debt or liability,
the amount that may be taken into account shall not
exceed the amounts included in the taxpayer’s net
worth on account of the assets serving as collateral for
the debt or liability.
(c) Debts and other liabilities of a taxpayer’s sole
proprietorship shall reduce net worth as if they were
debts or other liabilities of the taxpayer. The taxpayer’s
net worth shall not be reduced by the amount of debts
or other liabilities of a partnership, limited liability
company, or other business entity, other than a sole
proprietorship, that are allocated to the taxpayer for
purposes of computing tax, except to the extent that the
taxpayer is personally liable for that debt or other
liability.
(d) A taxpayer’s net worth shall not be reduced by the
taxpayer’s guarantee of another’s debts or other
liabilities.
(e) No debt or liability, including recourse debts
described in subdivision (a), shall reduce net worth if
the debt or liability is owed to a related person or
persons; if the existence or amount of the liability is
contingent on future events that are substantially
uncertain to occur or that are substantially uncertain to
occur within the subsequent five years; or if the debt or
liability was not negotiated for at arm’s length.
Additionally, no amounts shall be taken into account for
any debt or liability unless market rates of interest are
being charged to the taxpayer.
(f) A pledge to make a subsequent contribution to a
charitable or philanthropic organization shall not reduce
net worth unless that pledge is legally enforceable by
the organization to which that contribution is pledged,
and in any event no pledge may reduce net worth if that
pledge is entered into after October 15, 2025.
(g) Any debts or liabilities of a taxpayer in exchange for
which the taxpayer is entitled to receive future benefits
or future ownership rights, including a contractual
obligation to contribute to an entity at a future date,
shall only reduce net worth to the extent that:
(1) The value of those future benefits or ownerships
rights is included in the taxpayer’s net assets.
(2) The taxpayer can demonstrate, through clear and
convincing evidence, that the amount owed under the
debt or liability is in excess of any future benefits or
ownership rights that are not included in the taxpayer’s
net assets.
(3) In the case of a legally enforceable pledge to make
a subsequent contribution to a charitable or
philanthropic organization, the value of any future
benefits received in exchange shall be zero, except to
the extent that those benefits would constitute a
substantial benefit for purposes of determining the
contributor’s charitable contribution deduction.
